name: Liam Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at Kessler & Bright, an agency of eight in an old warehouse by the ring road. We do brochures, product catalogues and trade-show stands for engineering firms: pumps, valves, forklift parts. My day is mostly InDesign, setting up eighty-page catalogues so the part numbers line up in the grid. Once a month I go to the printer's for a press check, which is when you stand by the machine and approve the colour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like order. A catalogue where every table lines up is a quiet kind of satisfying. What wears me out is when an engineer changes a spec sheet after we've sent it to print. I don't use any AI tools, I just never got into them, and Doris, my manager, doesn't push it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I never saw what the fuss was about. At work I'd say we carry on as we were. I'm not really one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved. I'm not a fast designer and I'm still learning. If nothing big changes, I've got years to get better at catalogue layout and maybe move up to mid-level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Kessler & Bright, the same as now. I'd ask Doris if I can do more press checks, because I like the printer's floor. Ana and I would keep saving for a flat deposit, about four hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Steady. I like steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI did take some routine tasks, which bits of your day would it touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the catalogue tables, pulling part numbers from spreadsheets. Someone younger than me would set that up, I suppose. I'd let them, as long as I still check the pages before they go to print.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries outside of AI in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices, mostly. Ana teaches at the primary school on Birch Road, so her job's steady, and I'm on good pay for a junior. We've got about seven months saved and my car's paid off. We're fine, just slow getting to a deposit.

say: I'd say **fair enough**, I never saw the fuss.
At work I'd say we **carry on** as we were.
think: I'm **relieved**, because I'm a slow junior who's still learning.
A quiet world gives me **years to improve** and move up.
do: Keep working at the agency **as now**.
Ask my manager for **more press checks** at the printer.
Save about **four hundred** a month towards a flat deposit.
S0.quote: If nothing big changes, I've got years to get better at catalogue layout and maybe move up to mid-level.
fieldNote: He values **order and steadiness**, and has never used AI tools.
His partner's **teaching job** and a paid-off car keep the household secure.
His only pressure is **house prices** slowing the deposit.

steps.text: Keep laying out engineering catalogues at Kessler & Bright
Ask Doris for more monthly press checks at the printer
Save four hundred a month towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress and you can't stop it, that's how it's always been. At work I'd say let's see how the clients react first. I wouldn't make a speech about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. Catalogue layout is exactly the sort of task software does: data in, pages out. If Kessler & Bright can make a catalogue in a day with one person checking, they don't need two juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd wait a few months to see what Doris decides. If she starts using AI for catalogues, I'd ask to move to the trade-show side, the stand builds, because that's half hands-on. And I'd stop eating out so much and put that money into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My job could shrink, and I'm not someone who switches fast. But we've got savings and Ana's job is steady, so I'm not desperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't learning the tools protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'd be learning from scratch, and the kid they'd hire would be faster at it than me. I'd rather be good at something else than bad at the same thing everyone does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Petra, the other junior. She's quicker than me but she's renting alone. If one of us goes, I'd almost rather it was me, since I've got Ana. That's not a nice thing to think about.

say: I'd say it's **progress** and you can't stop it.
At work I'd suggest we **see how clients react** first.
think: **Catalogue layout** is exactly the task software does well.
A day's catalogue with one checker means **two juniors** aren't needed.
do: Wait a few months to see what my **manager decides**.
Ask to move to **trade-show stand builds**, which are half hands-on.
Stop eating out and move that money into **savings**.
feel: **Anxious**, because he's **slow to switch**, though savings soften it.
S1.quote: I'd rather be good at something else than bad at the same thing everyone does.
fieldNote: He prefers **waiting** to see what his manager does before acting.
He'd move towards the **hands-on stand building** rather than learn AI.
He shows quiet **concern for a colleague** renting alone.

steps.text: Wait to see if Doris brings AI into catalogue work
Ask to move to trade-show stand builds
Cut restaurant meals and save the difference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody saw it coming this fast, and governments will need to step in. At work I'd say let's be straight about who's staying. I'd probably say less than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the design side of my job is gone by 2028. Layout, catalogues, all of it. I'd have three years on the trade-show stands before robots, if that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Doris straight away to move me to stand builds full-time, setting up exhibition stands in halls. I'd do a forklift licence and a basic carpentry course in the first year. Ana and I would put the flat deposit on hold and keep the savings as a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. I don't do well with fast change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means if I'm building stands with my hands, I'm useful until about 2031. After that, I don't know. Maybe Ana's school still needs a caretaker, I'm only half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the flat's on hold, and that I'm sorry. She'd say it's fine, she'd say we've got her salary. But I wanted my partner and me to buy a flat before 30, and that would be gone.

say: I'd say **nobody saw it** coming this fast, and I'd say less than most.
I'd say governments will **need to step in** with help.
think: The **design side** of my job is gone by 2028.
I'd get **three years** on trade-show stands before robots, if that.
do: Ask my manager to move me to **stand builds** full-time.
Take a **forklift licence** and a basic **carpentry** course in year one.
Put the **flat deposit** on hold and keep savings as a buffer.
feel: **Alarmed** and lying awake, because he can't handle **fast change**.
S2.quote: I wanted my partner and me to buy a flat before 30, and that would be gone.
fieldNote: Speed forces him to act, despite his **resistance**.
He relies on his partner's **teacher salary** as the household anchor.
Losing the **flat-before-30** goal hurts more than the job itself.

steps.text: Ask Doris for a full-time move to exhibition stand builds
Get a forklift licence and take a basic carpentry course
Put the flat deposit plan on hold
Rely on Ana's teaching salary for the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say governments need a plan. With five years, I'd say they've got no excuse not to have one. At work I'd say we should talk about it at the Christmas meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I know myself. With five years, I'd tell myself there's time, and I'd wait. Then 2030 would arrive and I'd still be laying out catalogues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to set a date: by the end of 2028, I'm on stand builds. I'd do the carpentry course in the evenings next year. Ana and I might still buy the flat, but a cheaper one, further out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. Not because five years is short, but because I don't trust myself to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Petra getting let go. Or Doris buying the software. Something I could see with my own eyes in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about after robots arrive around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 35. Maybe in something with people, like teaching assistant work, like Ana. I really don't know, and I won't pretend to.

say: I'd say with five years governments have **no excuse** for lacking a plan.
I'd raise it at the **Christmas meeting**.
think: I know I'd tell myself **there's time**, and then **wait**.
I'd still be laying out **catalogues** in 2030, with the deadline close.
do: Set a **deadline** of end 2028 to be on stand builds.
Buy a **cheaper flat** further out with my partner.
feel: **Alarmed**, because he **doesn't trust himself** to use the time.
S3.quote: With five years, I'd tell myself there's time, and I'd wait.
fieldNote: His alarm comes from **self-knowledge**, not the timeline.
He needs a **visible trigger** in the office before moving.
He's honest that **after 2034** he has no plan.

steps.text: Move to stand builds by the end of 2028
Take evening carpentry classes next year
Buy a cheaper flat further out with Ana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for most people to sort themselves out, if they start. I'd say that to friends. At work I'd say we've got time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I could ride it out a while. I'd be 37 by 2036. The design job goes, but I'd have years to drift into the stands and the printer's floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Kessler & Bright for five or six years. I'd do more press checks and stand builds until it's half my job. We'd buy the flat in the next two years, as planned. Then I'd see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but low-level. It's a long way off, and I'm good at not thinking about long-way-off things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'then I'd see'. Is that a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. It's how I deal with things. I'd move slowly, but at least I'd move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the agency in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training on the stand side. Doris paying for the carpentry course. And honesty, if she's going to cut us, tell us early.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough** for most to sort themselves out.
At work I'd say we've got **time** to do it properly.
think: I could **ride it out** a while, being 37 in 2036.
I'd **drift slowly** into stands and the printer's floor.
do: Stay at the agency **five or six years**.
Grow **press checks** and stand builds to half my job.
Buy the **flat** in the next two years.
feel: **Anxious** at a low level, being good at **not thinking** about distant things.
S4.quote: I'm good at not thinking about long-way-off things.
fieldNote: He admits **'then I'd see'** is not really a plan.
A decade lets him **keep the flat purchase** on track.
He wants **early honesty** from his manager about cuts.

steps.text: Stay at Kessler & Bright for five or six years
Build press checks and stand work up to half his job
Buy the flat with Ana within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm slow to change, and that one doesn't let you be slow. What would help is a proper apprenticeship in exhibition building or carpentry, paid, with someone teaching you on the job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who don't post online. Lots of us just get on with it. You don't hear from people like me who don't post online until the job's gone.

headlineQuote: You don't hear from people like me who don't post online until the job's gone.
portrait: Liam is a **junior designer** laying out engineering catalogues at an eight-person agency.
He **never uses AI**, likes order and steadiness, and dislikes **change**.
His partner's **teaching job** and solid savings anchor the household.
He moves towards **stand building** and carpentry rather than learning AI tools.
He fears he'd **wait too long** even with years of warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it doesn't let a slow person be slow.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** in exhibition building or carpentry, taught on the job.
